name: mountain

attributes.attribute: a place where divine force came to rest
a hag of the high hills, likely from pre-Celtic times
a low hill with a wide view that held royal power
a low hill that grew to be the sacred core of Ireland

sources: Monaghan, Patricia. The Encyclopedia of Celtic Mythology and Folklore. Checkmark Books, 2008.
text: The mountain was a sacred sign to the Celts. The old Celts read all of nature as the home of the divine. Divine force did not spread itself evenly over the land. It came to rest in special places. Wells, the heads of rivers, hills, and mountains all drew the force. Both were seen again and again as powers of the land. The Cailleach, a hag of the high hills of Ireland and Scotland, may reach back to pre-Celtic times. Some scholars think that the love of mountains grew up before the Celts came. High ground also held royal weight in Ireland. A summit gives a clear view of all around, and so shields a people in war. The Hill of Tara rose low yet saw far across the fields. Uisneach, a low hill nearby, grew to be the sacred center of the whole land.
objective: Document the mountain as a sacred sign.
key_results: Record the mountain as a resting place of divine force.
Record the Cailleach of the high hills.
Record the royal and sacred role of Tara and Uisneach.
